name: marketing-evidence-profile
purpose: Research profile for marketing, market sizing, consumer insight, business planning, theory/book grounding, survey evidence, and quantitative claims.

reader_guide.summary: Use this profile when a task needs marketer-style desk research, marketing theory from books or journals, survey-backed claims, market-size estimates, consumer behavior data, or quantitative evidence.
how_to_read: Read evidence_lanes first to decide which evidence families must be searched.
Use source_groups as search origins, not proof; open exact reports, methods pages, datasets, or book records before citing.
Use quantitative_evidence_fields whenever a number, percentage, ranking, market size, spend figure, or survey result is extracted.
Use quality_scoring to decide whether a source can support a claim or only serve as discovery/context.
Use recommended_search_sequences to choose a human-like search order by task type.
update_triggers: A marketing, consumer insight, market sizing, or go-to-market research task repeatedly needs stronger quantitative evidence.
A new survey source, public dataset, industry report, book index, or marketing journal becomes useful.
A source becomes stale, paywalled, unavailable, sponsored without methodology, or unreliable.
A repeated marketing plan lacks numeric provenance, survey methodology, or theory/book grounding.
Korean market research needs additional Korean public data, survey, or consumer review channels.

structure_rules.rule: Marketing research must separate theory/book grounding, survey evidence, public statistics, commercial market reports, platform data, and qualitative/user signals before synthesis.
structure_rules.reason: Each lane answers a different question and has different failure modes.

structure_rules.rule: Every extracted quantitative value must record unit, geography, timeframe, population/base, method, source, access date, and comparability notes when available.
structure_rules.reason: Marketing numbers are often reused out of context, which causes misleading plans.

structure_rules.rule: Survey claims must include method disclosure or be downgraded to weak evidence.
structure_rules.reason: Sample source, population, mode, weighting, field dates, and sponsor strongly affect interpretation.

structure_rules.rule: Books and classic frameworks can ground concepts and theory, but current market facts need fresh data or official statistics.
structure_rules.reason: Books are valuable for theory but can be stale for current market behavior.

structure_rules.rule: Commercial reports and vendor surveys must record sponsor, business model, methodology disclosure, sample, and paywall limitations.
structure_rules.reason: Industry reports can contain useful numbers but often mix evidence, sales positioning, and proprietary methods.

structure_rules.rule: Market sizing should triangulate at least three evidence families, normally official statistics, industry report data, and explicit assumptions or observed platform data.
structure_rules.reason: TAM/SAM/SOM claims are frequently modeled estimates, not directly observed facts.

field_guide.meaning: Evidence families that should be searched and kept separate before synthesis.
Reusable source origins for marketing theory, survey quality, public statistics, industry reports, books, and platform data.
Search order by marketing task type.
Fields to record for any extracted number or survey result.
Scoring dimensions for deciding whether a source supports a claim or only provides context.
Reusable shape for recording marketing evidence in plans, research notes, or evaluation inputs.

limits: Do not use as proof of current market size or current consumer behavior without fresh data.
Requires methodology disclosure and population fit.
May not map directly to target audience or product category.
Check sponsorship, methodology, paywall limits, and whether estimates are modeled.
Platform estimates may be modeled and not comparable across platforms.
Use as discovery or voice-of-customer signal, not standalone proof.

sequence: define target market, geography, time horizon, and decision question
search marketing theory and books for frameworks
search peer-reviewed marketing journals for empirical or methodological support
search public statistics for denominators and market context
search survey and panel sources for consumer or marketer attitudes
search industry reports for current category benchmarks
search qualitative/community/review sources for customer language and pain points
synthesize only after numeric provenance and source quality notes are recorded
define market boundary, buyer segment, geography, period, currency, and unit
collect official population, business, household, income, or industry denominators
collect at least one industry or commercial report with methodology notes
collect platform, transaction, search, or behavioral proxies when relevant
record assumptions and model formula explicitly
triangulate high, base, and low estimates and mark modeled values as estimates
search public survey sources first
open methodology pages before extracting survey claims
record population, sample, mode, field dates, weighting, sponsor, and question wording
compare with at least one independent survey or public statistic when available
downgrade findings with missing method disclosure to weak evidence
search book metadata through Google Books, Open Library, WorldCat, or publisher pages
search related peer-reviewed articles or DOI metadata through Crossref, AMA journals, OpenAlex, or Semantic Scholar
separate timeless theory from current market claims
use current survey, statistics, or market reports for present-day evidence
search Korean official statistics through KOSIS and relevant ministries when population or market baselines matter
search Korean consumer surveys and local market reports such as OpenSurvey when consumer behavior matters
search Naver Blog/Search, Naver Map, Kakao Map, or Korean communities when user language and local signals matter
cross-check global market reports only after Korean source coverage is recorded
record source limitations for sponsored posts, sample ambiguity, and local platform bias

survey_methodology_checks: Who sponsored and who conducted the research?
What sampling frame and recruitment method were used?
What method and mode of data collection were used?
What was the sample size and subgroup base for the reported number?
Was weighting used, and what variables were used for weighting?
What exact question wording produced the metric?
Are response rates, panel source, or online sample quality controls disclosed?
Can the number be compared with prior waves, or did methodology change?

quality_scoring.high_signal: official statistics agency, peer-reviewed journal, recognized survey organization, or disclosed primary data source
quality_scoring.weak_signal: anonymous blog, unsourced slide, press release without methodology

quality_scoring.high_signal: population, sample, mode, dates, weighting, instrument, sponsor, and limitations are disclosed
current publication and stable methodology across time
quality_scoring.weak_signal: old number reused without dates or method changes

quality_scoring.high_signal: source population matches the target market and segment
quality_scoring.weak_signal: global or U.S. source used for Korean market without caveat

quality_scoring.high_signal: independent or transparent sponsor with disclosed conflicts
quality_scoring.weak_signal: vendor-funded report directly selling the solution category

quality_scoring.high_signal: data table, API, downloadable dataset, appendix, or method document exists
quality_scoring.weak_signal: only a chart image or uncited claim exists

quality_scoring.high_signal: claim is consistent across official statistics, survey data, and market reports
quality_scoring.weak_signal: claim depends on one modeled estimate
